title: Fail-safe adaptive primary structural response at ordinary-building cost

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a building’s primary lateral structural system that controllably and reversibly changes its effective stiffness or damping as earthquake motion develops. Stiffness governs resistance to deformation; damping governs dissipation of motion energy. The target combines useful real-time adaptation, a safe response when external grid power fails, and a total installed structural-system cost no greater than a comparable local code life-safety alternative. This is a research target, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

The distinction depends on structural function. A controllable damper or tuned mass added to a conventional primary frame does not by itself meet the target. An adaptive brace could qualify if it performs the primary lateral-system function. Reversible adaptation must also be distinguished from stiffness changes caused by cracking, yielding, or other damage: the intended capability is controlled adjustment followed by recovery to a predefined baseline.

significance.text: As a conditional assessment, achieving this combination would make the primary system’s mechanical response an affordable design variable during an earthquake, extending the choices made before construction. The important distinction is deliberate control during motion; it does not require assuming that conventional structures have perfectly constant stiffness or damping. The scale of the advance would depend on how much useful control authority the system provides, how reliably it operates, and whether the combined capability extends beyond existing practice.

The direct consequence would be control over the primary system’s response, not an automatic guarantee of lower damage or immediate occupancy. Those benefits would require separate evidence that adaptation improves the relevant performance measures without unacceptable effects elsewhere. At ordinary-building cost, a dependable system could make adaptive response accessible beyond specialized projects, but cost parity and dependable operation remain conditions of that possibility.

Immediate occupancy after the design earthquake is a separate outcome that can also be pursued through passive structural systems. Seismic cloaking instead attempts to alter the transmission of incoming waves; it does not establish adaptive primary structural response. Extending the proposed principle to wind, blast, or impact would require additional development and validation because success under earthquake loading would not establish performance under those hazards.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved target is the combined building-scale capability: primary-system adaptation with useful mechanical authority, reversible operation, dependable behavior during power loss, and ordinary-building affordability. The supplied record does not establish that no existing system meets this combination. It identifies a coherent capability to investigate, while leaving its field-wide novelty and present unmet status unresolved.

The research attributes several implementation barriers to Dharmajan and AlHamaydeh’s structural-control review: system complexity, reliable measurements, actuator capacity, time delays, sensor placement, and model uncertainty. These describe the challenge of measuring a moving structure and applying appropriate control actions with sufficient capacity and timing. The research also reports concerns about active-control stability and power requirements. These are attributed background findings; the source index contains no retained document text with which to verify their wording or precise scope.

Engineering synthesis: the primary system would need a defined mechanical response when controllers, sensors, communications, or power become unavailable. Loss of grid power and loss of all usable energy are different conditions; a battery-backed system must specify its operating duration and its behavior after depletion. Low control power alone does not demonstrate adequate building safety. The design must also distinguish intentional adjustment from damage-induced changes and integrate hardware, controls, inspection, and maintenance without defeating the affordability objective.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies Neethu B. Dharmajan and Mohammad AlHamaydeh’s “State-of-the-Art Review of Structural Vibration Control: Overview and Research Gaps,” Applied Sciences 15(14), 7966, dated 17 July 2025. The research says its full HTML was inspected, but the supplied source index marks it as not captured and lists no artifacts. The validated review therefore could not independently inspect the document or verify the attributed passages. The following account preserves the research’s reported findings with that limitation; missing retained evidence is not evidence that the findings are false.

According to the research’s account of the 2025 review, active, hybrid, and semi-active structural-control systems have reached full-scale applications in actual structures. The same account reports implementation barriers involving cost, power dependence, mechanical complexity, sensing, delays, and uncertain models. Full-scale applications demonstrate a more advanced stage than laboratory concepts, but they do not establish how widely the systems have been adopted. They also do not, by themselves, demonstrate a primary adaptive lateral system meeting the combined safety, reversibility, and cost target.

The research reports that the review distinguishes active control, which can require substantial external power and can destabilize a structure when forces are applied incorrectly, from semi-active devices such as magnetorheological dampers, which use relatively low control power and may operate from batteries. It also attributes passive-like fail-safe characteristics to semi-active systems. Without retained source text, these statements’ qualifications and applicability to particular devices remain unverified. They should not be read as a guarantee that every semi-active installation is stable or safe under every failure condition.

The research’s attribution of complexity, reliable-measurement, and actuator-capacity obstacles to Jiang and Wang is indirect, through the 2025 review; their underlying paper was not separately opened. Likewise, the historical papers associated with Yao and Kobori were not reopened. No later search coverage is supplied to establish the field’s position as of 1 November 2026, and no retained building-scale demonstration or cost comparison establishes completion of CIV-12. The appropriate conclusion is that completion and current novelty remain unverified, rather than that the innovation has been achieved or proven absent.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: test the primary lateral system of a multi-storey residential or office building under specified design-level shake-table motions, or document its response during a suitably instrumented design-level earthquake. Measure a controlled change in effective stiffness or damping during motion and recovery to a predefined baseline afterward. Specify how those properties are estimated, account for measurement uncertainty, and distinguish commanded adaptation from damage-induced changes. Demonstrate useful control authority and achievement of predefined response objectives, rather than merely detecting a small property change.
completion_criteria.label: Building-scale primary system reversibly adapts and meets predefined response objectives

completion_criteria.text: Proposed power-loss comparison: remove external grid power at predefined points during testing and show, using declared safety measures and acceptance limits, that the building remains at least as safe as a comparable passive code life-safety alternative. Specify the backup-energy allowance, control duration, fallback mechanical state, and consequences of energy depletion. Separate tests of relevant sensor, controller, or actuator failures would strengthen the broader fail-safe claim. These are proposed evaluation boundaries, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Grid-power loss preserves safety relative to passive code life-safety alternatives

completion_criteria.text: Proposed affordability comparison: use the same building size, location, site conditions, loading assumptions, and comparable design requirements for the adaptive and passive alternatives. Include the installed primary structural system, sensors, controls, actuators, backup power, installation, and commissioning in the cost boundary. Report pricing dates and uncertainty. Report maintenance, inspection, replacement, and energy obligations separately so that first-cost parity is not mistaken for demonstrated lifetime affordability.
completion_criteria.label: Report comparable full installed costs and separate ongoing obligations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility evidence would include repeat motions, recovery measurements, disclosed configurations and control logic, accessible measurement records, and independent replication or verification. A single-degree-of-freedom specimen would be useful development evidence but would not meet the building-scale criterion. Neither would supplemental devices added to an otherwise conventional primary system. Tests spanning multiple motions and operating conditions would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not universal earthquake safety. Residual drift, damage, and reoccupancy should be reported separately and cannot substitute for measured reversible primary-system adaptation.
completion_criteria.label: Building-scale reversible primary-system adaptation is reproducible from disclosed evidence

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CIV-09, immediate building occupancy after the design earthquake at life-safety cost, is the closest overlap. CIV-12 concerns a controllable structural capability; CIV-09 concerns a post-earthquake performance outcome. An adaptive primary system might help meet CIV-09, but immediate occupancy requires separate evidence and may be achieved through passive approaches. CIV-04, repeated recovery of structural load capacity after cracking, concerns restoration after damage. Returning a commanded stiffness or damping setting to baseline does not itself demonstrate recovery of damaged load capacity.

Roster-based synthesis: CIV-02 concerns prediction of liquefaction and its ground consequences, while CIV-03 concerns converting ground into a specified engineering solid. Either could inform or support a building’s seismic design, but controlling its primary lateral system does not establish prediction or prevention of ground failure. CIV-06 concerns the cost of underground routes and spaces; any use of adaptive structural control underground would be a separate application requiring its own evidence.

Roster-based synthesis: CIV-01 addresses a structural binder without process carbon dioxide; CIV-05 addresses tensile-ductile mineral structures; CIV-07 addresses load-bearing engineered living materials; and CIV-11 addresses corrosion-free reinforcement with carbon-steel behavior at default cost. These concern materials, manufacture, durability, or economics that could influence an adaptive system’s construction. None establishes real-time primary-system adaptation, and CIV-12 does not require or demonstrate their respective breakthroughs.

Roster-based synthesis: CIV-10 concerns structural concrete storing building-relevant energy. Such storage could conceivably support controls or backup operation, but energy storage and fail-safe adaptive response remain separate capabilities. CIV-08 concerns reservoir sediment passage while preserving carryover water and has no direct technical overlap established here. These entries remain distinct; shared infrastructure use or possible future integration does not merge their completion criteria.

change_log.change: Preserved CIV-12’s identity and combined primary-system, reversibility, power-loss safety, and affordability target while qualifying its claimed absence from existing practice.
change_log.reason: The proposal is coherent, but the supplied evidence does not establish field-wide novelty or present unmet status.

change_log.change: Retained the research’s detailed account of full-scale control applications and engineering barriers as explicitly attributed findings, alongside the missing-artifact limitation.
change_log.reason: Useful technical content should survive consolidation without implying that the source was independently inspected during the validated review.

change_log.change: Replaced the categorical rejection of braces with a distinction based on primary structural function.
change_log.reason: An adaptive brace could perform the primary lateral-system function; the device name alone cannot determine eligibility.

change_log.change: Separated deliberate adaptation from ordinary response variation and damage-induced property changes.
change_log.reason: Conventional stiffness and damping need not be perfectly constant, and damage-related change does not demonstrate controlled reversibility.

change_log.change: Qualified broad claims about adoption and semi-active fail-safe behavior.
change_log.reason: Full-scale use does not establish adoption prevalence, and reported device characteristics do not guarantee safety for every installation or failure condition.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed demonstrations to define measurement baselines, useful control authority, cost boundaries, power-loss comparisons, and reproducibility.
change_log.reason: These definitions make the research target assessable while preserving the criteria as proposals rather than established standards.

change_log.change: Separated controllability from immediate occupancy and other hazard applications, and explained relationships across the supplied roster.
change_log.reason: Potential downstream benefits require their own evidence and should not merge distinct innovations.

unresolved_issues: No retained artifact permits independent verification of the 2025 review’s text, detailed qualifications, or bibliographic metadata; the research’s reported HTML inspection cannot substitute for that missing artifact.
No supplied search coverage establishes whether an existing primary adaptive system meets the combined target as of 1 November 2026.
A concrete design must define effective stiffness or damping, useful control authority, recovery tolerances, and how controlled change will be distinguished from damage.
Safety measures, passive comparison conditions, backup-energy duration, and the intended scope of failure tolerance remain unspecified.
The proposed cost comparison needs project-specific pricing and a final accounting boundary; lifetime affordability remains separate from installed-cost parity.
No supplied building-scale test, independent replication, or cost comparison demonstrates completion. The proposed test programme would establish performance only within its documented conditions.

brief.title: Buildings that adjust to earthquakes at ordinary cost
possible: People could live and work in buildings whose main structure adjusts as an earthquake unfolds. It would change how strongly it resists deformation or absorbs shaking, then return to a predefined baseline.

That response would remain safe when grid power fails. The complete installed structural system would cost no more than a comparable local alternative designed to meet building-code life-safety requirements.
why: Engineers could control a building’s response during an earthquake, extending the choices they make before construction. Affordable systems could bring that capability to ordinary homes and offices, beyond specialized projects.

sources.who: Neethu B. Dharmajan and Mohammad AlHamaydeh
sources.showed: This review surveys systems that control structural vibration, their use in actual structures, and barriers to implementation.
sources.cited_for: It supports the background on existing structural control systems and their practical obstacles.
sources.not_established: Existing applications do not establish the combined target of reversible primary structural adjustment, power-loss safety and ordinary-building cost.

sources.who: Qinyu Wang, Gennaro Senatore, Kaspar Jansen, Arjan Habraken and Patrick Teuffel
sources.showed: Heated joints reduced shaking in a small frame. Repeated loading showed that viscoelasticity, deformation that absorbs energy, improved ductility, the ability to deform without breaking.
sources.quote:
Through cyclic testing, it has been observed that material viscoelasticity is beneficial to ductility and 
energy dissipation.
sources.cited_for: The experiments support adjusting structural response through joints that change their mechanical properties.
sources.not_established: A small prototype does not establish building-scale recovery, safety during power loss or comparable installed cost.

shown: Qinyu Wang and colleagues tested heat-controlled joints in a small frame on a shaking platform. Changing the joints’ resistance to deformation and ability to absorb motion reduced the frame’s response to earthquake loading.

Structural control systems have also reached actual buildings. Neither that experience nor the small-frame tests establish the complete combination of primary structural adjustment, recovery, power-loss safety and affordability.
missing: A building-scale demonstration must establish useful, controlled adjustment and recovery, distinct from changes caused by damage.
Power-loss tests must establish safety against a comparable conventional design, including after backup energy runs out.
A complete installed-cost comparison must include the structure, controls, sensors, powered devices and backup power.
Independent replication must establish that building-scale results can be reproduced.

milestones.label: A building-scale structure adjusts and recovers
milestones.explanation: A building-scale test would have to meet predefined response goals through controlled adjustment and return to baseline afterward. This would establish useful adaptation rather than damage.

milestones.label: Safety holds when grid power fails
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to show safety at least matching a comparable conventional code-compliant design during grid-power loss, with backup limits defined. This would establish dependable behavior when power fails.

milestones.label: Full installed costs match a comparable conventional system
milestones.explanation: A like-for-like comparison would have to show installed-cost parity, with ongoing obligations reported separately. This would establish initial affordability without confusing it with lifetime cost.

milestones.label: Building-scale adjustment and recovery can be reproduced
milestones.explanation: Repeated building-scale tests and disclosed measurements and control logic would have to support independent replication or verification. This would establish reproducibility across the tested conditions.

uncertain: Whether any existing system already meets the complete target remains unresolved.
Useful adjustment, recovery tolerances and acceptable safety comparisons still need precise definitions.
Reduced damage and immediate occupancy would need separate proof; controlled structural adjustment alone does not establish them.
